questions.title: Encapsulated Entity with Accessor Methods
questions.question: Implement a `Student` class demonstrating standard encapsulation by declaring private fields `name` and `age` alongside public getters and setters, and test state access in `main`.
questions.explanation: Encapsulation is a foundational object-oriented principle that restricts direct external access to an object's internal representation while exposing a controlled public interface[cite: 10]. Marking member fields with the `private` access modifier ensures they are completely hidden from code outside the declaring class[cite: 10]. Public accessor (`getName()`, `getAge()`) and mutator (`setName()`, `setAge()`) methods act as guarded gateways[cite: 4, 10]. Mutators allow developers to enforce invariants, sanitize inputs, or reject illegal arguments before updating internal heap fields[cite: 10]. Direct field manipulation bypasses these validation guarantees, coupling callers directly to internal representation details[cite: 10].
hints: Declare `private String name;` and `private int age;` inside the class body[cite: 4, 10].
Implement public accessor methods returning the fields, using lower camelCase naming[cite: 4, 10].
Use `this.name = name;` in mutators to disambiguate shadowed parameters from instance fields[cite: 4, 6, 10].
questions.expectedOutput:
Student name: Akshat
Student age: 26

questions.title: Intra-Class Field Accessibility Matrix
questions.question: Declare member variables demonstrating all four access levels (`public`, `protected`, default package-private, and `private`) in a class, and verify that an internal member method can access all four levels directly.
questions.explanation: Java specifies four levels of member visibility: `public`, `protected`, default (package-private, denoted by omitting any access modifier keyword), and `private`[cite: 10]. Regardless of the access modifier assigned to an instance variable, the declaring class itself always possesses full, unrestricted access to all of its own members[cite: 10]. Member methods executing within the class context read and write private, default, protected, and public fields with equal privilege because lexical boundaries are evaluated at the class level rather than at individual method instances[cite: 10]. Access restrictions only apply when external types attempt to access those members across class or package boundaries[cite: 10].
hints: Declare four separate fields with distinct modifiers: `public`, `protected`, default (no keyword), and `private`[cite: 10].
Write an instance method `displayAll()` within the same class that reads and formats each field[cite: 10].
Instantiate the class in `main` and invoke the method to verify full intra-class visibility[cite: 10].

Accessing from inside declaring class:
Public: PUBLIC
Protected: PROTECTED
Default: DEFAULT
Private: PRIVATE

questions.title: Co-Package Member Visibility Collaboration
questions.question: Create two classes residing in the same package to verify that default (package-private) and `protected` members of one class are accessible from the other without subclassing.
questions.explanation: In Java's access model, both package-private (default) and `protected` members grant unrestricted access to any other class residing within the same declared package namespace[cite: 10]. A class declared in package `com.demo` can instantiate another class in `com.demo` and directly read its default and protected fields or invoke its default and protected methods without requiring inheritance[cite: 10]. The key distinction between the two modifiers appears only outside the package: `protected` members remain accessible to subclasses in foreign packages, whereas package-private members are completely inaccessible outside their package boundary[cite: 10].
hints: Declare a collaborator class with `protected String protectedMsg;` and `String defaultMsg;`[cite: 10].
Instantiate the collaborator class inside the caller within the same file or package[cite: 1, 10].
Access both fields directly using dot notation (e.g., `collaborator.defaultMsg`)[cite: 10].

Read default: Default Package Data

questions.title: Static Factory Instantiation with Private Constructor
questions.question: Implement a class that restricts instantiation by declaring its constructor `private`, and provide an explicit public static factory method `create()` to generate valid instances.
questions.explanation: Declaring a constructor `private` prohibits client code from using the `new` operator directly from outside the class body[cite: 10]. This pattern is central to the Static Factory Method pattern (Joshua Bloch, Effective Java)[cite: 10]. Instead of uncontrolled instantiation, the class provides a public static method (often named `create()`, `of()`, or `getInstance()`) that controls how instances are created, validated, or cached[cite: 5, 10]. Static factories allow meaningful method names, can return existing cached instances, and can even return subtype implementations without exposing internal constructor details to consumers[cite: 10].

questions.title: Private Helper Method Delegation
questions.question: Write a class that exposes a public method for client invocation, which internally delegates sub-tasks to a private helper method to prevent internal implementation leaks.
questions.explanation: Separating public API methods from private helper routines is fundamental to high-cohesion, low-coupling software architecture[cite: 10]. A public method establishes the external contract expected by callers, performing high-level coordination[cite: 10]. Private helper methods break down complex workflows into manageable, reusable steps (such as input sanitization, checksum validation, or low-level parsing) without exposing internal mechanics[cite: 10]. Marking helpers `private` prevents client code from depending on implementation details, allowing internal logic to be refactored safely without breaking external API contracts[cite: 10].
hints: Declare `private String sanitize(String input)` to perform lower-level string transformations[cite: 10].
Declare `public String processInput(String raw)` that invokes `sanitize(raw)` internally[cite: 10].

Declaring `balance` private prevents external code from directly corrupting account state (such as assigning negative balances or bypassing transaction logging)[cite: 10]. The public `deposit(double amount)` mutator guards modifications with a validation check: if an invalid non-positive amount is supplied, the method rejects the operation with an error message[cite: 10]. A read-only public getter provides access to the balance without giving callers the ability to modify it[cite: 10].

questions.title: Package-Private Visibility Test

questions.explanation: In Java, omitting an explicit access modifier (`public`, `protected`, or `private`) designates the member as package-private (often referred to as default visibility)[cite: 10]. Package-private members are visible to every class compiled within the exact same package namespace[cite: 10]. Unlike `public`, default members are completely hidden from classes residing in other packages, including subclasses[cite: 10]. This makes package-private access ideal for modular framework design, where internal utility classes collaborate within a package without exposing their methods to the public API[cite: 10].

questions.title: Protected Member Access via Subclass

questions.explanation: The `protected` access modifier bridges package-level encapsulation and object-oriented inheritance[cite: 10]. A protected member is accessible to all classes within the same package, as well as to subclasses regardless of the package in which they reside[cite: 10]. When a child class extends a parent containing a protected method, the child inherits the method as part of its own member space[cite: 10]. The subclass can call the method directly (`super.initProtected()` or `initProtected()`), enabling extensible library designs where parent classes provide protected hooks for subclasses to customize behavior[cite: 10].

By exposing only a single public method (such as `executePipeline()`) while marking all intermediate routines (`validate()`, `transform()`, `persist()`) as private, the class presents a clean, unambiguous interface to external callers[cite: 10]. This prevents external code from depending on internal helper routines, ensuring internal algorithms can be updated, optimized, or refactored without breaking downstream consumers[cite: 10].

questions.title: Private Constructor Instantiation Blocker

questions.explanation: Utility classes (such as `java.lang.Math` or `java.util.Collections`) provide static utility methods and are never intended to be instantiated[cite: 5, 9, 10]. If a class does not declare an explicit constructor, the Java compiler automatically generates a default public zero-argument constructor, allowing unwanted instantiation[cite: 10]. Declaring a `private` constructor prevents client code from using the `new` operator[cite: 10]. Throwing an `AssertionError` inside the private constructor provides an additional defense against internal calls or reflective instantiation bypasses, ensuring the utility class remains non-instantiable under all conditions[cite: 10].

questions.explanation: Protected visibility is designed to support controlled inheritance across package boundaries[cite: 10]. If class `Parent` in package `a` defines a `protected void execute()` method, an unrelated class in package `b` cannot invoke `parentInstance.execute()`—the compiler rejects it with an access violation error[cite: 10]. However, if class `Child` in package `b` extends `Parent`, it inherits the protected method into its subclass scope[cite: 10]. The child can invoke the method using `super.execute()` or direct method calls, enabling extensible framework architectures across separate packages[cite: 6, 10].

questions.title: Protected Member Target-Type Invocation Rule

A subclass `Child` extending `Parent` across packages can access the protected field on `this` or on other `Child` instances[cite: 10]. However, `Child` cannot access the protected member on a plain `Parent` reference (`parentInstance.protectedField`)[cite: 10]. This rule prevents one subclass from inspecting or altering the protected state of other unrelated subclasses or parent instances in external packages[cite: 10].

To enforce this, the constructor must be declared `private`, preventing client code from instantiating secondary objects via `new`[cite: 10]. In multithreaded environments, a double-checked locking idiom with a `volatile` static instance field guarantees thread safety while avoiding synchronization overhead on subsequent reads[cite: 6]. The `volatile` modifier prevents CPU instruction reordering during instantiation, ensuring other threads never observe a partially constructed object reference[cite: 6].

questions.title: Immutable Value Object via Private Final Fields
questions.question: Write an immutable `GeoPoint` class with private final fields, no setters, and constructor-based initialization to guarantee thread-safe state immutability.
questions.explanation: Immutable objects provide inherent thread safety because their internal state cannot be modified after construction[cite: 5, 6]. Designing an immutable class requires four key rules: 1) Declare the class as `final` to prevent subclasses from adding mutable state[cite: 5]. 2) Declare all member fields as `private final` so their references or primitive values cannot be modified[cite: 5, 6, 10]. 3) Omit setter methods entirely[cite: 10]. 4) If fields hold mutable object references, return defensive copies from getters[cite: 10]. Because the fields are permanently assigned during object construction, multiple threads can share instances concurrently without synchronization locks[cite: 6].

Initialize all fields exclusively within the constructor[cite: 6].

questions.title: Package-Private Helper Class Decoupling

A top-level class can only be declared `public` or default (package-private)[cite: 1, 10]. When a class is declared without the `public` modifier, it is completely invisible outside its compilation package[cite: 10]. Public classes within that package can instantiate and use the package-private helper freely, but external packages cannot see or import it[cite: 10]. This pattern helps maintain clean package boundaries by preventing internal utility classes from leaking into external APIs[cite: 10].

questions.title: Cross-Package Protected Inheritance Restriction
questions.question: Demonstrate cross-package protected access boundaries: show that a subclass in another package can access a protected parent variable via `this`, but cannot access it through an external instance of the parent class.
questions.explanation: Java's protected access rules can surprise developers because `protected` is not purely package-private plus public inheritance[cite: 10]. Under JLS §6.6.2, when accessing a protected member outside its package, access must occur within a subclass body, and the target object must be of that subclass type (or one of its subtypes)[cite: 10]. If class `Sub` in package `pkg2` extends `Super` in package `pkg1`, inside `Sub`, accessing `this.protectedVar` or `super.protectedVar` is legal[cite: 6, 10]. However, attempting `new Super().protectedVar` inside `Sub` fails at compile time because `Super` is not a subtype of `Sub`[cite: 10].

questions.title: Immutable Value Object via Modifiers and Defensive Copying
questions.question: Build an immutable `User` class with private final fields, no setters, a package-private constructor, and defensive copying in getters for mutable fields like `java.util.Date`.
questions.explanation: Creating truly immutable objects requires defensive copying whenever mutable reference types (such as `java.util.Date` or arrays) are used[cite: 5, 10]. Even if a field is declared `private final`, returning the internal mutable reference directly (`return this.createdAt;`) allows callers to mutate the internal object state via `createdAt.setTime(0)`[cite: 5, 6, 10]. To prevent this leak, the constructor must make a defensive copy of incoming mutable arguments, and getters must return new copies (`return new Date(this.createdAt.getTime());`)[cite: 5, 10]. This guarantees that external callers cannot corrupt the object's internal state[cite: 10].

questions.title: Eager and Lazy Singleton Instantiation Controls
questions.question: Implement both an eager Singleton and a lazy Singleton class, using `private` constructors to prevent client code from creating secondary instances.
questions.explanation: The Singleton pattern controls instantiation using access modifiers[cite: 10]. In an eager Singleton, the instance is allocated statically when the class is loaded into memory (`private static final Singleton INSTANCE = new Singleton();`), providing thread-safe initialization without synchronization overhead[cite: 6, 10]. In a lazy Singleton, the instance is deferred until `getInstance()` is called, using double-checked locking with a `volatile` field to ensure safe initialization across threads[cite: 6]. In both patterns, declaring a `private` constructor ensures external classes cannot instantiate secondary objects using the `new` operator[cite: 10].

However, `WidgetFactory` resides in the same package, so it can invoke the package-private constructor freely[cite: 10]. External packages can then create widgets only through `WidgetFactory.createWidget()`, allowing the factory to enforce validation, object pooling, or configuration without exposing constructor details[cite: 10].

questions.explanation: Interfaces in Java follow strict modifier rules defined in JLS §9.3 and §9.4[cite: 10]. Any field declared inside an interface is implicitly `public static final`, even if those keywords are omitted[cite: 10]. Attempting to declare a field as `private`, `protected`, or non-final causes a compile-time error[cite: 10]. Similarly, standard interface methods are implicitly `public abstract`[cite: 10]. While Java 8 added `default` and `static` methods and Java 9 added `private` helper methods, regular interface methods remain public and abstract[cite: 10]. questions.title: Private Reflection Bypass and Security Risks
questions.question: Use Java Reflection (`setAccessible(true)`) to read and modify a `private` field from outside its class, and explain in comments why this bypass undermines security and compiler optimizations.
questions.explanation: Java's core Reflection API (`java.lang.reflect`) allows inspecting classes, methods, and fields at runtime[cite: 2]. By obtaining a `Field` reference and invoking `field.setAccessible(true)`, code can suppress standard Java language access control checks, allowing it to read and modify `private` fields from external classes[cite: 10]. While useful for frameworks (such as dependency injection engines and ORMs like Hibernate), bypassing encapsulation this way breaks object invariants, risks data corruption, and can be blocked in modern runtimes by the Java Module System (`--illegal-access=deny`)[cite: 10].

questions.title: Inner and Outer Bidirectional Private Access

questions.explanation: In Java, an inner class and its enclosing outer class share the same nestmate context (formalized in Java 11 via JEP 181 Nest-Based Access Control)[cite: 10]. Under JLS §8.1.3, an inner class has access to all members of its enclosing class, including `private` fields and methods[cite: 10]. Conversely, the outer class has full access to the `private` members of its inner class instances[cite: 10]. Prior to Java 11, the compiler generated package-private synthetic bridge methods (`access$000`) to enable this access; modern JVMs support nestmate access natively in bytecode with `invokevirtual` and `invokespecial`[cite: 10].

questions.title: Method Overriding Visibility Widening
questions.question: Override a `protected` method from a parent class as `public` in a subclass. Explain why widening visibility is allowed while narrowing visibility (e.g., overriding as `private`) causes a compilation error.
questions.explanation: Under the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) and JLS §8.4.8.3, an overriding method cannot reduce the visibility of the method it overrides[cite: 10]. If a parent class declares a method `protected`, a subclass can keep it `protected` or widen it to `public`[cite: 10]. However, the subclass cannot narrow visibility to package-private or `private`[cite: 10]. Allowing a subclass to narrow visibility would break polymorphism: a caller holding a parent reference (`Parent p = new Child()`) expects to be able to call the method, which would fail if the subclass restricted access[cite: 6, 10]. Widening access is safe because it preserves or expands the parent's contract[cite: 10].

questions.title: Subclass Method Visibility Widening
questions.question: Demonstrate that an overriding method can widen visibility (`protected` to `public`) but cannot reduce visibility (`public` to `private`), and explain the compiler's type-safety rules.
questions.explanation: When a subclass overrides a parent method, the Java compiler enforces access rules to preserve polymorphism and type safety (JLS §8.4.8.3)[cite: 10]. A subclass can expand member access (e.g., overriding package-private as `protected` or `public`, or overriding `protected` as `public`)[cite: 10]. However, narrowing access (e.g., overriding `public` as `protected` or `private`) causes a compilation error[cite: 10]. Under polymorphism, an instance of a subclass can be assigned to a parent reference (`Parent p = new Child()`)[cite: 6]. If the subclass could narrow access, calling `p.publicMethod()` would fail at runtime, violating polymorphic substitutability[cite: 10].

questions.title: Private Interface Method Encapsulation
questions.question: Write an interface containing two public `default` methods that share common validation logic extracted into a `private` interface method (introduced in Java 9).
questions.explanation: Java 8 introduced `default` methods in interfaces, allowing interfaces to provide concrete method implementations[cite: 10]. However, when multiple default methods shared common logic, developers often had to duplicate code or leak helper methods into the public interface API[cite: 10]. Java 9 resolved this by adding support for `private` methods inside interfaces[cite: 10]. Private interface methods can be either static or non-static, can be called by default or static interface methods, and are completely hidden from implementing classes and consumers[cite: 10]. This enables clean code reuse inside interfaces without polluting public API contracts[cite: 10].

questions.title: Package Boundary Encapsulation Auditing Engine
questions.question: Implement an auditing utility using Java Reflection that inspects a target class and verifies whether any package-private class inadvertently exposes `public` constructors or mutable fields.
questions.explanation: In large enterprise codebases and library frameworks, encapsulation leaks can occur when internal classes inadvertently expose public constructors or public fields[cite: 10]. While a package-private class cannot be imported directly outside its package, declaring public constructors on it can cause design smells and create unintended access paths via reflection or subclassing[cite: 10]. An automated reflection auditor inspects classes at runtime: if a class is not declared `public`, it examines its declared constructors and fields using `getModifiers()`, flagging any members that carry `public` modifiers and verifying that package boundaries remain clean[cite: 10].
